summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client send several commands at once instead of waiting for a reply to each one. A server advertises that it supports this. It makes mail delivery faster, especially over slow links.

plainLanguage.summary: SMTP pipelining lets a client send several commands before waiting for their replies. It uses this option only after the server advertises support, and the replies remain in command order.

subtitle: How an SMTP client can send command groups without waiting after every command.

tldr.problem: SMTP's one-command-at-a-time exchange makes clients wait repeatedly for replies, which is costly on high-latency links.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises the PIPELINING extension in its successful EHLO response. The client may then send eligible commands in a group, and the server responds in command order.
tldr.outcome: The RFC's example reduces client/server turnarounds from 9 to 4. RFC 2920 is STD 60 and obsoletes RFC 2197.

today: RFC 2920 is an Internet Standard (STD 60) that obsoletes RFC 2197. No later RFC is listed as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Why SMTP Pipelining Helps
sections.content:
SMTP normally pairs each command with a server response. On a high-latency connection, waiting for each response can dominate the time needed to send a message.

Not all SMTP servers can safely handle commands sent together. The RFC describes problems such as losing data buffered during a process handoff, flushing input after an error, or making incorrect assumptions about how earlier recipient commands affect DATA. Pipelining is therefore an advertised SMTP extension, not an assumption a client can make for every server.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting for a reply after every mail command adds delay when a network is slow. A client can send commands in groups, but only when the server says it supports that behavior.

sections.title: The PIPELINING Announcement
sections.content:
The extension is named Pipelining and the EHLO keyword is PIPELINING. It has no parameter, adds no parameter to MAIL FROM or RCPT TO, and defines no new SMTP verb.

A client first sends EHLO. If the server responds with code 250 and includes the PIPELINING keyword, it has declared that it can handle pipelined commands. The client may then send groups without waiting for each individual response.
sections.plainLanguage: The client checks the server's EHLO response for PIPELINING. If the successful response includes that word, the client may use command groups.

sections.title: Client Rules for Command Groups
sections.content:
RSET, MAIL FROM, SEND FROM, SOML FROM, SAML FROM and RCPT TO may appear anywhere in a group. EHLO, DATA, VRFY, EXPN, TURN, QUIT and NOOP may appear only as the final command because their result changes the state the client must handle. NOOP can be used as a synchronization point.

A pipelining client must check every command's response. It matches responses to commands by counting them and must support multiline responses; it must not match by response code or text. A client that cannot process replies while still transmitting must ensure the entire group fits within the TCP window to avoid deadlock.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands that do not change the next step can be grouped freely, while state-changing commands must end a group. The client counts replies to match each one to its command.

sections.title: Server Requirements
sections.content:
A server offering pipelining must answer commands in the order received. It should buffer responses for groups of commands such as MAIL FROM and RCPT TO, but must not buffer responses to EHLO, DATA, VRFY, EXPN, TURN, QUIT, NOOP or unrecognized commands.

The server must send pending responses whenever its local TCP input buffer is emptied. It must not assume commands that have not yet arrived, and must never flush or lose input-buffer contents. It should accept DATA only when a valid RCPT TO address was received, and its response text should identify the command where practical.
sections.plainLanguage: The server replies in the same order as the commands arrived. It must preserve commands already received and must not guess what the client will send later.

sections.title: Example Dialogue and Turnarounds
sections.content:
The RFC compares an ordinary SMTP exchange with one that uses pipelining. In the ordinary exchange, the client waits for the server 9 times. In the pipelined example, it sends MAIL FROM, three RCPT TO commands and DATA as a group, then sends the message terminator and QUIT together. The number of turnarounds falls to 4.

The RFC also shows why clients must check each response: a server may reject every recipient but still incorrectly accept DATA. The client must handle that DATA response rather than assuming its result from the RCPT TO replies.
sections.plainLanguage: In the RFC's example, grouping mail commands cuts the waits from 9 turnarounds to 4. Clients still need to read each reply because command failures can affect later steps.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not discuss security issues and says that pipelining is not believed to introduce issues beyond those already present in electronic mail and in fully conforming implementations of RFC 821.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC identifies no new security issue caused by command pipelining beyond the existing risks of electronic mail.
